To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the world's farmers, particularly in the developing countries, would be substantially better off, and the world would be better off economically, with lower levels of poverty and inequality, if the governments of the rich countries reduced their agricultural protection and the developing-country governments reduced their agricultural subsidies and import barriers, as well as their nonfarm trade barriers.

the world's poorest people would be better off if agricultural policies in the rich countries were liberalized, if the poor countries were allowed to liberalize their own agricultural policies, and if rich-country farm subsidies were used instead to reduce poverty and inequality through more direct means.

The world's poorest billion people would be better off if agricultural and nonagricultural policies in all countries were changed to reflect the principle that the best policy for a country's poorest is to pursue policies that maximize the country's economic growth, and the poorest billion would be better off still if, as a result of the changes, world economic growth were increased.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of agricultural price distortions on global poverty, the distribution of poverty across countries, and the distribution of income and poverty across households within countries.

two key policy questions: What would be the effect of eliminating all distortions to agricultural prices and trade in the world economy, and what would be the effect if the same policy change were to be accompanied by an equalizing transfer of resources?

the effects of agricultural price and trade policies and their interactions with nonagricultural policies on the welfare and distributional consequences of agricultural policies, and on the incidence and distribution of poverty.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of farm price and trade policies are complex, and that the effects on the distribution of poverty depend on the initial conditions and on the nature of the policies.
the global and individual country studies have provided a strong case for the importance of agricultural trade and price policies for reducing poverty in developing countries.
agricultural price and trade policy reform would reduce poverty, increase economic growth, and improve income distribution in all regions of the world.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of price and trade distortions are large, and that these effects are not uniform across regions, countries, or within countries.
agricultural price distortions, especially in developing countries, are associated with higher rates of poverty and greater inequality in poverty.
the policies that have been pursued by governments in the more well off countries, and by governments in the less well off countries, have reduced global economic welfare and increased poverty.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in general, reducing agricultural price distortions and trade barriers can have a large positive impact on poverty and inequality.
the effects of price and trade policies are large.
the effects of farm price and trade policy distortions on poverty and inequality are significant, and that these effects are large enough to warrant policy reform.
